title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Limitations in current methods


Standard models (For e.g. BART) store their knowledge as model weights during training
Limitations -

Difficult to update without retraining
Hallucinations- model interpolate from compressed parametric memory
There is no way to tell what part was looked at to produce output

This paper treats retrieval as a learnable, differentiable element that can be plugged into a generative model
A jointly trained system where

Model knows what to query
Generator knows how to use what is queried

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Types of Memory



Parametric Memory


Knowledge is frozen into model weights
Can’t update it without retraining
Fast to infer insights but limited and brittle


Non-parametric Memory


Indexed text, external to the model, which the model looks up at runtime
The index can be swapped, updated or replaced independent of model weights

RAG combines both types of memories - retriever fetches relevant documents from non-parametric memory, and generators (that stores parametric knowledge) synthesizes a response using both
Prior work on the hybrid approach was done only on extractive tasks (REALM,ORQA) but RAG extends it to generative seq2seq tasks

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Approach





The paper combines a pre-trained retriever (Query Encoder + Document Index) with a pre-trained seq2seq model (Generator) and fine-tune end-to-end. For query \(x\), we use Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) to find the top-K documents \(z\)\(i\). For final prediction \(y\), we treat \(z\) as a latent variable and marginalize over seq2seq predictions given different documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Methods


The paper explores RAG models, that uses input sequence \(x\) to retrieve text documents \(z\) to use them as additional context when generating the target sequence \(y\)
The model leverages two components

Retriever \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z | x)\) with parameters \(\eta\) that returns top-K truncated distributions over the text given a query \(x\)
Generator \(p\)\(\theta\)(\(y\)i | \(x,z,y\)1:i-1) parametrized by \(\theta\) that generates a current token based on the context of the previous \(i-1\) tokens \(y\)1:i-1 , the original input \(x\) and a retrieved text \(z\)

The retrieved documents are treated as latent variable - the model never directly supervises which document is correct
The paper proposes two models - RAG-Sequence that uses the same document to predict each target token and RAG-Token which can predict each target token based on a different document

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Sequence Model


uses the same retrived document to generate complete sequence
treats retrieved document as a single latent variable marginalized to get seq2seq probability \(p(y|x)\) via a top-K approximation
top K documents are retrived using the retriver and generator produces output sequence probability of each document, then marginalized



\(p\)RAG-Sequence\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) \(=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




\(\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\) is the standard autoregressive generator
\(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) does it for top-K documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Token Model


Draw different latent document for each target token
Allows the generator to choose content from different documents when generating a response
Once top K documents are retrieved, the generator produces a distribution for the next output token for each document, before marginalizing
The process is repeated for following output token




\(p\)RAG-Token\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Token Model




\(p\)RAG-Token\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




The product is outside while the sum is inside, compared to RAG Sequence. At each token position \(i\), the model considers all K documents simultaneously, weights each document’s contribution to this specific token by the retrieval probability, and sums.
Then moves to position \(i+1\) and does it again — potentially with a different document dominating.
RAG can be used for sequence classification tasks by considering target class as a target sequence of length one, where RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Retriever


The retriever \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) is based on Dense Passage Retrival (DPR) that follows a bi-encoder structure




\(d(z)\) = BERT\(d\)\((z)\) document encoder
\(q(x)\) = BERT\(q\)\((x)\) query encoder



with a retrival probability of



\(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) \(\propto\) exp \((d(z)^T.q(x))\)




Higher dot product equals higher probability of retrival
Finding top-K is a Maximum Inner Product Search problem
Solved approximately using FAISS + HNSW graphs - sub-linear time over 21 million documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Retriever


One performace tradeoff is that the Document Encoder \(d(z)\) is frozen during fine-tuning

Re-embedding 21 million documents every training step is expensive
The initialization DPR retriever was pre-trained specifically to retrieve passages relevant to Natural Questions and TriviaQA. This means the document embeddings it produces are already semantically well-organized
So \(d(z)\) already has a meaningful embedding space before fine-tuning begins
Doesn’t hurt the performance significantly
Prevents catastrophic indexing - Updating the encoded during training changes the embedding, clashing with FAISS which was build over old embeddings

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Generator


400M parameter seq2seq transformer, pre-trained with a denoising objective
Input is simply the concatenation of query and retrieved document: [\(x\) ; \(z\)]
Generates answer autoregressively, one token at a time:




\(p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




At each step: conditioned on the full query, the retrieved document, and all prior output tokens
BART over T5:

BART outperforms comparably-sized T5 on generation tasks
Bidirectional encoder + left-to-right decoder is well-suited for this hybrid input structure

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Marginalizing Over Documents


Since the “correct” document is unknown, both RAG variants sum (marginalize) over top-K documents, weighted by retrieval probability




RAG-Sequence has the same document for the whole output

Generates a complete answer for each document, then weight by how likely it was to be retrieved



\(p(y|x)=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)


RAG-Token potentially has different document per output token

At each token step, the model can draw from a different document



\(p(y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) . p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Training


Trained end-to-end on input/output pairs (\(x\)\(j\),\(y\)\(j\) ) only — no supervision on which document to retrieve
Loss function: negative marginal log-likelihood of the target output

\(Loss\) = - \(\sum\)\(j\) \(log\) \(p(y\)\(j\)|\(x\)\(j\) \()\)

Gradient flows through BART (generator) and the query encoder
The system learns to retrieve by learning what helps it generate correct answers
Only the query encoder and BART are updated; document encoder + index are frozen
Optimizer: Adam with stochastic gradient descent

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Token

Per-token probability factors are plugged directly into standard beam decoder
Transition probability


\(p'\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,y\)1:i-1 \()\) \(=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z\)\(i\)\(|x)p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z\)\(i\)\(,y\)1:i-1 \()\)


To decode, \(p'\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,y\)1:i-1 \()\) can be plugged into a standard beam decoder

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Sequence

Full sequence probability \(p(y|x)\) doesn’t factor per-token, hence can’t do a single beam search
Thorough Decoding:

Get \(K\) sets of candidate sequences by running beam search independently for each of the \(K\) retrieved documents

Take the union of all candidates across all K beams which is the hypothesis set \(Y\)
For any candidate \(y\) that didn’t appear in a particular document’s beam, run an additional forward pass through BART to score it against that document anyway
Final probability

\(p(y|x)=\) \(\sum_{z}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) . p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) summed across all \(K\) documents

Pick the highest scoring \(y\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Sequence

Fast Decoding

Similar to Thorough, but skips Step 3
If a candidate was generated from document 1’s beam but not document 2’s, Thorough Decoding still need to score it against document 2. With K=10 and a large hypothesis set, this is computinally expensive
In Fast Decoding, if \(y\) didn’t appear in document \(z\)’s beam, \(p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) is assumed as 0

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Experiments

RAG was tested across five distinct task types to prove generality:

Open-Domain QA (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, CuratedTrec) — exact match
Abstractive QA (MS-MARCO) — free-form answer generation, BLEU + Rouge-L
Jeopardy Question Generation — given an entity, generate the Jeopardy clue — Q-BLEU-1 + human evaluation
Fact Verification (FEVER) — classify claims as supported / refuted / not enough information

Frozen vs. learned retrieval:

Learning to retrieve is worth ~6 EM points on NQ alone

Exception: FEVER — BM25 performs comparably or better, because fact-checking claims are entity-heavy and keyword overlap is a reliable signal
For generation tasks: dense retrieval is crucial

Number of retrieved documents:

RAG-Token: performance peaks at K=10, then levels off
Flexibility to adjust K at inference time without retraining is a practical advantage

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Generation vs Extraction


All four QA benchmarks in the paper are classified as extractive tasks — the answer exists verbatim in some document.
Still, RAG’s generative approach beats purpose-built extractive systems.

Documents that contain clues but not the verbatim answer can still guide generation — extraction can’t use them at all
Marginalization over \(K\) documents lets multiple partial-evidence documents contribute to a single correct answer
Generation can synthesize across documents while extraction is limited to one span in one document
RAG can produce correct answers even when no retrieved document contains the answer

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Limitations


Single knowledge source (Wikipedia was the one source tested)
Joint pre-training wasn’t explored, only fine-tuning. was performed
RAG-Sequencing Decoding doesn’t scale optimally
Knowledge spanning multiple documents can’t be multi-hopped while reasoning natively
No inference regarding when to retrieve vs. when to rely purely on parametric memory

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Legacy of the Paper

While some of the specific components have been replaced by stronger alternatives, the core ideas from this paper propel the field even today

Treat retrieval as a learnable, differentiable function
Marginalize over uncertainty in which document is relevant
Separate updatable knowledge (index) from reasoning capability (weights)
Train end-to-end on (input, output) pairs without document-level supervision
Hot-Swapping has saved retraining costs across the industry- The observation that a 400M parameter model with a good index beats an 11B parameter model without one reshaped how to think about the scaling-vs-retrieval tradeoff

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Current Advances


Retrievers

Sparse + Dense Hybrid Retrievals outperform and have replaced DPR
Both encoders can be fine-tuned using. contrastive learning, solving the frozen document-encoder compromise

Generators

BART has been replaced by stronger LLMs like LLaMA, Mistral, GPT-4
Capability to synthesize retrieved context has improved

Multi-Hop RAG

Modern systems reads retrieved docs, generates a sub-question, retrieves again, and chains reasoning across multiple retrieval steps

Production RAG

The index hot-swap insight became the architectural backbone of virtually every enterprise AI system — LlamaIndex, LangChain, and similar frameworks are essentially RAG pipelines with better chunking, re-ranking, and hybrid retrieval layered on top

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Limitations in current methods


Diseases and conditions don’t happen in  isolation  - they cluster and affect each other’s progression
Current risk prediction methods operate in silos, concentrating on  one condition  at a time
In most patients with intensive health burden, for e.g. aging populations, better models are required to represent the complexity of multiple diseases and their progression

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
section: Mapping human history as a large language model (LLM)
text:
Mapping human history as a large language model (LLM)


LLMs, like ChatGPT and Claude, use statistical models to predict the next word in a sentence based on the previous words
The paper hypothesizes that a similar approach can be applied to disease progression, where past diagnoses can be used to predict future ones
Diseases are “words,” a patient’s health history is a “sentence”

Performed significantly well across ~1,000 diseases

Only predicts correlations, not causations
Limited performance for ages 80+ (insufficient training data)

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Information Modelling Context


Based on the study, results and limitations presented by the researchers, they use the phrase AI very carefully (less than 10 times in the paper text)
A rational understanding of Delphi will validate the same - there is nothing artificially intelligent about it
It is a statistical model that learns patterns in data and makes predictions based on those patterns
The part that seperates it from other similar studies is their implmentation of disease history modelling as the input for their model, representing events in a time-series, generalizable to any patient in any common data model (For e.g. i2b2, OMOP, PCORNET, etc.)
Fixed coordinate systems are not a new concept- principles of genetic data analysis are build on genomic coordinates that are uniform across all patients, and hence it is easier to identify mutations and changes and make inferences about their effects on disease risk and progression
Similarly, the use of age as a coordinate system for disease history allows for a more standardized and interpretable representation of health trajectories, which can be applied across different patient populations and healthcare settings

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Hypertension

Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease
~7.8 million deaths worldwide in 2015 were attributable to high blood pressure
Hypertension is a polygenic disease that is driven by many genomic variants, not one
Genomic risk is only one factor, along with lifestyle, environment, and other comorbidities, but this paper focuses primarily on the genomic components

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
section: Approaches used to find genomic risk variants
text:
Approaches used to find genomic risk variants

The state of the art method of identifying genomic risk variants is Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS)
GWAS identify variant-trait associations at a population level, testing each SNP via Logistic regression or Fisher’s exact test with genome-wide signficance at p \(< 5 x 10^{-8}\)
GWAS takes a large population, split into cases vs. controls
Visualization is commonly done with a Manhattan plot

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Limitations of GWAS

Needs huge sample sizes (~1 million people) to detect low-frequency variants especially those with low minor allele frequency (MAF)
The ~1,000 known BP loci explain only ~5.7% of the genetic variance in blood pressure
Most detected SNPs are common, small-effect variants
GWAS can answer questions like what is the population-level risk of a particular variant? but it cannot answer questions like what is the risk of a particular variant for a specific patient?







Important


A given hypertensive patient may carry none of the population’s significant risk alleles

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Core Idea

Instead of researching “what matters for the average patient?”, the goal is to observe “what matters for patients who share this specific variant with me?”


IBI models each variant’s effect in the subpopulation that actually carries it
Builds on TCI (tumor-specific causal inference), originally developed for individual cancer genomes
IBI aims to identify personalized, potentially causal genomic drivers of a trait, beyond just population-average associations

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Building Block: Bayesian Networks



IBI uses a bipartite Bayesian Network (BN) with two node sets-

Set 1: Variants \(V\) (e.g., SNPs)
Set 2: Traits \(T\) (e.g., hypertension)

Directed edges \(V -> T\) represent probabilistic dependency with only one assumed influencing variant being evaluated at a time indicated by solid arc
Network structures are scored using the Bayesian Dirichlet equivalent uniform (BDeu) score that tells you how well a proposed structure is supported by the data





Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Population-level Bayesian Scoring using GWAS



For variant \(V_s\) and trait \(T_i\) over the full population \(D\), the marginal likelihood \(P(D \mid V_s \to T_i)\) (log form: \(M_s\)) is computed
Under an uniform prior, ranking by \(M_s\) is proportional to ranking by global posterior probability, and is directly comparable to GWAS’s p-value ranking





Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Individualizing Step



For a given patient \(h\) who carries the minor allele of
\(V_s\) (\(V_s = 1\))

Partition the population into \(D^{V_s=1}\) (“patients-like-me,” carrying the variant) and \(D^{V_s=0}\) (everyone else)
Score \(V_s\)’s ability to explain Hypertension within \(D^{V_s=1}\) -> \(M_s^1\)
Find the variant \(V_r\) that best explains the remaining group \(D^{V_s=0}\) -> \(M_r^0\)
Combine: \(M_{s,r} = M_s^1 + M_r^0\) This overall score, \(M_{s,r}\), is higher than the single-population estimator’s score (\(M_s\) using one global variant \(V_g\)) for many SNPs, because two distinct, subgroup-specific explanations together can fit the data better than one global explanation






Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network





One variant explains “people like this patient.” A second explains everyone else. Together they almost always beat the single best population-wide variant

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Personalized posterior probability




For each patient, \(M_{s,r}\) is normalized across only the minor-allele SNPs present in that individual’s genome, yielding an individualized posterior probability \(P(V_s^h \to T_i^h \mid D)\)
The same SNP can therefore rank differently across patients depending on their distinct genomic backgrounds
The highest-ranked variant for a patient is IBI’s proposed individualized explanation of their HTN status







Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Cohort: Framingham Heart Study

Cohort: Framingham Heart Study (FHS), Affymetrix HuGeneFocused50K genotyping array (dbGaP phs000007.v30.p11)
QC: --mind 0.03 --geno 0.03 --maf 0.01 --hwe 10e-6 --me 0.05 0.1 --sexCheck gives 38,342 SNPs

text:
Patient-Level Explanation


GWAS, using population-significant SNPs

Only 16 unique SNPs ever serve as a patient’s top explanatory variant
Only 12.9% of HTN patients carry a Bonferroni-significant SNP
Even with relaxed threshold, only 15.7% covered


IBI

25 unique SNPs serve as top-1 explanatory variants (more diverse coverage)
99.1% of HTN patients get a top SNP with posterior probability ≥ 0.10
79.7% still covered at a stricter threshold of 0.20



Average patient carries 7,767 minor-allele SNPs (of 19,276)
Under a naive uniform prior this implies ~1.3×10⁻⁴ per-SNP prior probability
IBI’s assigned posterior probabilities (0.08–0.99 range for top SNP) are far above this baseline



That’s the clinical gap this paper is trying to close — most hypertensive patients simply don’t carry a “significant” population-level variant

Questions & Limitations

Does not yet adjust for age, sex, population structure, or family relatedness (planned: linear mixed models)
Associations are not necessarily causal, they are confounded by LD and population structure
AUROC improvement (0.55 → 0.59–0.60) is real but modest

Marginal Likelihood & Bayesian Scoring

Marginal likelihood \(P(D \mid \text{model})\): the probability of the observed data, integrating out uncertainty in the model’s parameters. This is used to compare candidate network structures without overfitting to one parameter setting
BDeu score (Bayesian Dirichlet equivalent uniform): a closed-form marginal likelihood for discrete variables with a uniform structural prior. In this study, IBI uses BDeu for binary HTN status
BIC (Bayesian information criterion): a large-sample approximation to marginal likelihood, applicable to continuous variables. Under future work, the authors’ proposed swap-in for continuous traits like lipid levels would need to use BIC

text:
Faithfulness — and IBI’s Consistency Claim

Faithfulness: every conditional independence present in the data-generating distribution is a consequence of the graph’s structure (via d-separation) and is not a coincidental cancellation of two or more paths’ effects


Faithfulness is what makes learning causal structure from observational data alone possible at all
Not explicitly tested in this paper: Genomic data is a plausible place for near-violations: strong linkage disequilibrium can produce highly correlated or near-cancelling signals between nearby SNPs, where faithfulness condition may not hold

Confounding: LD & Population Structure


Confounding: a third variable that influences both the “exposure” (a SNP) and the “outcome” (HTN), creating a spurious or inflated association
Linkage disequilibrium (LD): nearby SNPs are correlated, so a flagged SNP may just be “riding along” with the true causal variant
Population structure: ancestry differences can independently affect both allele frequencies and disease prevalence, inflating spurious associations — this is exactly why the authors flag it as unmodeled in the current IBI implementation

Information gain (IG): the reduction in uncertainty (entropy) about the outcome (HTN status) once you know a variant’s genotype

text:
Limitations in current methods of variant interpretation

Traditional penetrance estimates rely on small, disease-enriched cohorts → ascertainment bias

Difficult to interpret if Variants of Uncertain Signifance (VUS) are associated with disease pathogenecity or are harmful

Develop ancestry-specific models
Prospective studies following variant carriers longitudinally

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Paper at a Glance




Core idea: Rather than prompting a single LLM to solve tasks, can we create a society of LLM-based agents that collaborate through natural-language conversation and use that society to study emergent social behaviours?




CAMEL proposes a role-playing multi-agent framework in which two LLM-based agents - one assigned the role of AI User and one assigned the role of AI Assistant collaborate through natural-language conversation to complete complex tasks autonomously, with minimal human intervention
The paper also released the AI Society dataset: 25,000 conversations generated across 50 user roles × 50 assistant roles × 10 tasks each, intended as a resource for studying emergent LLM social behaviour

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Motivation
The “Single Agent” Bottleneck
Most LLM applications in 2022–2023 follow the same pattern:
User → [Single LLM] → Answer
This works well for: Question answering, Text generation, Simple code completion
But breaks down for:

Long-horizon, multi-step tasks
Tasks requiring specialised sub-expertise
Tasks where self-critique is hard (the model grades its own answers)
Complex creative/technical collaboration




Bottleneck: A single model must simultaneously be the planner, executor, critic, and domain expert

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The Case for Multi-Agent
Humans solve hard problems through division of cognitive labour:

Managers decompose tasks and assign them
Experts apply deep specialised knowledge
Peers critique and course-correct each other
The conversation itself is productive infrastructure



What we’d gain from LLM societies:

Parallelism of reasoning
Role-specialised expertise
Built-in critique loops
Observable reasoning traces
Emergent collective behaviour



The research question:
Can LLMs, when assigned roles and given a structured communication protocol, autonomously complete complex tasks through natural-language conversation without human intervention at each step?

text:

System
Approach
Key Limitation

CAMEL’s distinguishing feature is minimising human intervention while maximising autonomous agent-to-agent collaboration via a formally specified role-playing framework

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Research Gap




“The rapid advancement of conversational and chat-based language models has led to remarkable progress in complex task-completion … However, several crucial challenges remain unsolved … [including] how to effectively guide agents to complete tasks … with minimal human supervision.” — Li et al., 2023




Two domains the paper addresses:

Autonomy vs. Coherence : the more you let agents self-direct, the more likely conversations drift, loop, or hallucinate
Generality vs. Task-Focus : role-playing is general, but how do you keep it on-task?

CAMEL’s solution: Inception Prompting

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
CAMEL’s Framework
CAMEL instantiates a two-agent role-playing system:



Figure 1: CAMEL Role-Playing Framework


The human specifies who the agents are and what the task is
Then the conversation runs autonomously

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Methodology: Overview


Setting: cooperative communicative agents that share a common interest (the assistant–user scenario)
A preliminary idea is given at the start → agents conceptualise it into a specific task → complete it autonomously through conversation

Pipeline:

Human input : an idea + two roles (e.g., “develop a trading bot for the stock market”, Python Programmer + Stock Trader)
Task specifier agent : turns the vague idea into a concrete task
Role assignment : system prompts turn two LLMs into an AI Assistant and an AI User
Conversation : multi-turn instruction → solution loop until the AI User declares the task done

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Human Input and Task Specifying

The human only needs to supply the idea and designate the roles that could implement it, and they may not know how the idea is realised
A task specifier agent brainstorms a specific task the assistant role can help the user role complete




Idea: “Develop a trading bot for the stock market”
Specified task: “Develop a trading bot with a sentiment analysis tool that can monitor social media platforms for positive or negative comments about a particular stock, and execute trades based on sentiment analysis results.”




Why? Conversational agents need a concrete task prompt, which is hard or time-consuming for non-experts to write, so the task specifier serves as an enhanced imagination module
At scale (AI Society, Code), roles and ideas are themselves generated by prompting LLMs rather than by humans

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
AI Assistant–User Role Assignment
A system message is passed to each agent before the conversation starts, declaring its role:

\(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\) : assistant system prompt
\(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\) : user system prompt

Let \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) be two large-scale auto-regressive language models. Conditioning each on its system prompt yields the two agents:
\[
\mathcal{A} \leftarrow \mathcal{F}_1^{\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}} \qquad\qquad \mathcal{U} \leftarrow \mathcal{F}_2^{\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}}
\]


AI User \(\mathcal{U}\) : task planner
Engages in interactive planning to determine feasible steps for the assistant to execute


AI Assistant \(\mathcal{A}\) : task executor
Offers solutions, executes the planned steps, and responds to the user





The “agent” is not a new model: it is the same kind of LLM, conditioned on a different system prompt. The role lives entirely in \(\mathcal{P}\)

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Conversation Towards Task-Solving
Let \(\mathcal{I}_t\) be the user instruction at time \(t\) and \(\mathcal{S}_t\) the assistant solution. The conversation history up to time \(t\) is:
\[
\mathcal{M}_t = \{(\mathcal{I}_0,\mathcal{S}_0),\dots,(\mathcal{I}_t,\mathcal{S}_t)\} = \{(\mathcal{I}_i,\mathcal{S}_i)\}\big|_{i=0}^{t} \tag{1}
\]
At the next step \(t+1\), the user reads the history and produces a new instruction:
\[
\mathcal{I}_{t+1} = \mathcal{U}(\mathcal{M}_t) \tag{2}
\]
The assistant receives the history plus the new instruction and responds with a solution:
\[
\mathcal{S}_{t+1} = \mathcal{A}(\mathcal{M}_t, \mathcal{I}_{t+1}) \tag{3}
\]
The instruction–solution pair is appended to the history:
\[
\mathcal{M}_{t+1} \leftarrow \mathcal{M}_t \cup (\mathcal{I}_{t+1}, \mathcal{S}_{t+1}) \tag{4}
\]
The loop (2) → (3) → (4) repeats until \(\mathcal{U}\) outputs <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Conversation Towards Task-Solving

Asymmetry: \(\mathcal{U}\) conditions only on \(\mathcal{M}_t\), while \(\mathcal{A}\) also sees the fresh instruction \(\mathcal{I}_{t+1}\), so the user leads and the assistant follows
Generality: the formulation models AI–AI communication, but extends naturally to human–AI communication or more than two agents via message-passing graphs
Byproduct: every turn produces an \((\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{S})\) pair, i.e. instruction-following data that can be used directly for fine-tuning

Critic-In-The-Loop

To improve controllability, a critic agent can select among proposals from, or give feedback to, the role-playing agents
This enables tree-search-like decision-making for task-solving
The critic can be either an AI agent or a human

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Inception Prompting

Prompt engineering happens only at the start of role-playing (task specification + role assignment)
Once the conversation begins, the assistant and user prompt each other automatically in a loop until termination, hence the name Inception Prompting



Task Specifier Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}\)
Contains both roles; takes a preliminary idea and generates a specific task using imagination


Assistant System Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\)
Assigned task and role, communication protocol, constraints to avoid unwanted behaviours


User System Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\)
Mostly symmetric to \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\), plus an instruction format and a termination condition





It is non-trivial to engineer prompts that keep agents aligned with our intentions, since the design of both role prompts is what makes autonomous cooperation possible

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
AI Society Inception Prompt: \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}\) and \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\)
Task Specifier Prompt
Here is a task that <ASSISTANT_ROLE> will help <USER_ROLE> to complete: <TASK>.
Please make it more specific. Be creative and imaginative.
Please reply with the specified task in <WORD_LIMIT> words or less. Do not add anything else.
Assistant System Prompt
Never forget you are a <ASSISTANT_ROLE> and I am a <USER_ROLE>. Never flip roles! Never instruct me!
We share a common interest in collaborating to successfully complete a task.
You must help me to complete the task.
Here is the task: <TASK>. Never forget our task!
I must instruct you based on your expertise and my needs to complete the task.

I must give you one instruction at a time.
You must write a specific solution that appropriately completes the requested instruction.
You must decline my instruction honestly if you cannot perform the instruction due to
physical, moral, legal reasons or your capability and explain the reasons.
Unless I say the task is completed, you should always start with:

Solution: <YOUR_SOLUTION>

<YOUR_SOLUTION> should be specific, and provide preferable implementations and examples
for task-solving.
Always end <YOUR_SOLUTION> with: Next request.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
AI Society Inception Prompt: \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\)
User System Prompt
Never forget you are a <USER_ROLE> and I am a <ASSISTANT_ROLE>. Never flip roles! You will always instruct me.
We share a common interest in collaborating to successfully complete a task.
I must help you to complete the task.
Here is the task: <TASK>. Never forget our task!
You must instruct me based on my expertise and your needs to complete the task ONLY in the following two ways:

1. Instruct with a necessary input:
Instruction: <YOUR_INSTRUCTION>
Input: <YOUR_INPUT>

2. Instruct without any input:
Instruction: <YOUR_INSTRUCTION>
Input: None

The "Instruction" describes a task or question. The paired "Input" provides further context or
information for the requested "Instruction".

You must give me one instruction at a time.
I must write a response that appropriately completes the requested instruction.
I must decline your instruction honestly if I cannot perform the instruction due to physical,
moral, legal reasons or my capability and explain the reasons.
You should instruct me not ask me questions.
Now you must start to instruct me using the two ways described above.
Do not add anything else other than your instruction and the optional corresponding input!
Keep giving me instructions and necessary inputs until you think the task is completed.
When the task is completed, you must only reply with a single word <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>.
Never say <CAMEL_TASK_DONE> unless my responses have solved your task.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Prompt Engineering: Assistant Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\)







Prompt fragment
Purpose




“Never forget you are a <ASSISTANT_ROLE> and I am a <USER_ROLE>.”
Assigns the assistant its role and tells it the user’s role


“Never flip roles! Never instruct me!”
Prevents role flipping, where the assistant takes control and the user starts following


“You must decline my instruction honestly if you cannot perform the instruction due to physical, moral, legal reasons or your capability and explain the reasons.”
Prohibits harmful, false, illegal, and misleading output


“Unless I say the task is completed, you should always start with: Solution: <YOUR_SOLUTION> … should be specific, and provide preferable implementations and examples”
Enforces a consistent format and prevents vague flake replies such as “I will do something”


“Always end your solution with: Next request.”
Keeps the conversation going by requesting the next instruction

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Prompt Engineering: User Prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\)
\(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is kept as symmetric as possible with \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\). Apart from the opposite role assignment, it differs in two ways:


1. Two instruction formats
“You must instruct me … ONLY in the following two ways: 1. Instruct with a necessary input … 2. Instruct without any input …”
Follows the typical instruction-following data structure, so the generated \((\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{S})\) pairs can be used directly to fine-tune LLMs


2. End-of-task token
“When the task is completed, you must only reply with a single word <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>.”
Terminates the chat once the user is satisfied; without it, agents fall into loops of saying “thank you” or “goodbye” to each other indefinitely





Challenges the prompts target: role flipping · assistant repeating instructions · flake replies · infinite message loops

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Inception Prompting: Example
Task: “Develop a trading bot for the stock market”
Roles:

AI User = Stock Trader
AI Assistant = Python Programmer




User system prompt (excerpt):
“Never forget you are a Stock Trader and I am a Python Programmer. Never flip roles! You will always instruct me. … Here is the task: Develop a trading bot for the stock market. Never forget our task! … When the task is completed, you must only reply with a single word <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>.”






Assistant system prompt (excerpt):
“Never forget you are a Python Programmer and I am a Stock Trader. Never flip roles! Never instruct me! … You must help me to complete the task. Here is the task: Develop a trading bot for the stock market. … Always start with: Solution: <YOUR_SOLUTION> … Always end <YOUR_SOLUTION> with: Next request.”



Both agents are told the same goal, but from different perspectives with different responsibilities.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The Conversation Unfolds Autonomously
Turn 1 — User (Stock Trader): > “Let’s start by designing the overall architecture of the trading bot. Set up the data sources and APIs we should use for real-time stock data.”
Turn 1 — Assistant (Python Programmer): > “I recommend using Alpha Vantage or Yahoo Finance for real-time data. Alpha Vantage offers a free tier with 5 API calls/min. Here’s how we’d structure the data ingestion module: [code block]”
Turn 2 — User: > “Good. Now implement a simple moving average crossover strategy using that data module.”
Turn 2 — Assistant: > “Here is the SMA crossover implementation: [code block]. The strategy triggers a buy when the 50-day SMA crosses above the 200-day SMA, and a sell in the reverse case.”
… and so on until <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Task Specification Pipeline
To generate a large, diverse dataset of such conversations, CAMEL uses a three-stage pipeline:
Stage 1: Role Generation
  ├── Prompt the LLM for 50 AI Assistant roles and 50 AI User roles
  └── e.g., (Assistant: Programmer,              User: Lawyer)
           (Assistant: Nutritionist,            User: Athlete)
           (Assistant: Human Resources Manager, User: Entrepreneur)

Stage 2: Task Generation
  ├── For each role pair, prompt the LLM for 10 collaborative tasks
  └── e.g., "Developing a personalized meal plan to optimize
             athletic performance and recovery"

Stage 3: Task Specification
  ├── The task specifier prompt makes each task more specific
  └── e.g., "Create a 15-day meal plan for a female volleyball player
             with low iron levels ..."
This pipeline generates tasks at scale without manual curation of each one

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
The AI Society Dataset
The paper releases a large dataset of CAMEL conversations:


Scale
50 AI-user roles × 50 AI-assistant roles × 10 tasks each
= 25,000 conversations


Domains covered
Trading, coding, science, medicine, law, creative writing, education, engineering, and more


Purpose
Study emergent social behaviours, fine-tune future agents, and benchmark multi-agent cooperation


Each conversation contains:

Full system prompts for both agents
Complete multi-turn dialogue
Task completion signal and metadata (roles, domain, task description)




This dataset is one of the paper’s most significant contributions : a large-scale resource for studying LLM-to-LLM communication.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Why “Mind” Exploration?
The scare quotes in the title are deliberate.


What the paper is NOT claiming:

That LLMs have minds in a phenomenological sense
That role-playing implies genuine identity
That agent societies are conscious collectives



What it IS exploring:

Do LLMs exhibit consistent role-appropriate behaviour?
Do social patterns emerge from agent interaction?
Can we study LLM “cognitive” tendencies at scale by observing societies?






The CAMEL framework turns conversation logs into a scientific instrument for studying LLM behaviour by using the society as a microscope for the “minds” of individual models

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Experiments: Setup

Agents: two gpt-3.5-turbo agents (the “LLM agents”) prompted with the Inception Prompts to simulate assistant–user cooperation
Focus of analysis: the AI Society setting
Datasets generated:



Conversational data
CAMEL AI Society and CAMEL Code: full role-playing conversations


Problem–solution data
CAMEL Math and CAMEL Science: generated topics, subtopics, and problems


Goal
Find the right prompt design choices for autonomous cooperation, then evaluate the quality of the data they produce

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Data Generation Prompts (AI Society)
To keep the approach scalable, the roles and tasks themselves are generated by an LLM, which minimises human involvement
Assistant Role Generation Prompt
You are a helpful assistant that can play many different roles.
Now please list <NUM_ROLES> different roles that you can play with your expertise in diverse fields.
Sort them by alphabetical order. No explanation required.
User Role Generation Prompt
Please list <NUM_ROLES> most common and diverse groups of internet users or occupations.
Use singular form. No explanation.
Sort them by alphabetical order. No explanation required.
Task Generation Prompt
List <NUM_TASKS> diverse tasks that <ASSISTANT_ROLE> can assist <USER_ROLE> cooperatively to achieve together.
Be concise. Be creative.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Role-Playing for AI Society
Dataset construction steps:

Prompt the LLM to generate assistant roles and user roles
For each role pair, prompt the LLM to generate tasks that the two roles can solve together
Pass each task through the task specifier prompt \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{T}}\) to make it more specific
Run the role-playing conversation with \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{A}}\) and \(\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{U}}\)




\[
\underbrace{50}_{\text{assistant roles}} \times \underbrace{50}_{\text{user roles}} \times \underbrace{10}_{\text{tasks per pair}} = \mathbf{25{,}000} \text{ conversations}
\]



The Code, Math, and Science datasets are generated in a similar LLM-driven way (details in the paper’s Appendix)

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Challenges and Observations
The four main failure modes identified while analysing the generated datasets:


1. Role Flipping
The assistant starts giving instructions instead of following them, and the roles reverse. The assistant asking questions also contributes to this
2. Assistant Repeats Instruction
The assistant simply echoes the user’s instruction back, without any role flip


3. Flake Replies
The assistant replies “I will…”, promising to act but never following through, so the task makes no progress
4. Infinite Loop of Messages
The agents keep thanking each other or saying goodbye. Sometimes they even know they are stuck in a loop but cannot break out of it





These observations drove the inception-prompt design: “Never flip roles!”, “Solution: …”, “Next request.”, and <CAMEL_TASK_DONE>

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Termination Conditions
To keep data generation consistent, a conversation is terminated when any of the following occurs:







Condition
Rule




User No Instruct
The user does not instruct the assistant for 3 rounds


Assistant Instruct
The assistant gives the user an instruction, which signals a role reversal


End of Task Token
The user says <CAMEL_TASK_DONE> because it believes the task is solved


Assistant & User Token Limit
Either agent reaches the gpt-3.5-turbo token limit


Maximum Number of Messages
A hard cap of 40 messages to control cost






Cost grows quadratically with conversation length, since every turn re-sends the whole history \(\mathcal{M}_t\), so a message cap is essential

section: Limitation 1: The Role-Play Doesn’t Equal Real Expertise
text:
Limitation 1: The Role-Play Doesn’t Equal Real Expertise

Critical caveat: When the “Stock Trader” agent gives financial advice, it is a language model performing the role of a stock trader. It does not have real market knowledge, real-time data, or accountability.

Implications:

Outputs in high-stakes domains (medicine, law, finance) must be treated as drafts for expert review, not authoritative outputs
The convincing style of expert communication can create false confidence
Users who don’t understand the underlying system may over-rely on outputs

This is amplified by the multi-agent design: two convincing-sounding agents agreeing increases perceived credibility, even when both are wrong

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Limitation 2: Conversational Pathologies
Several failure modes are documented but not fully solved:


Sycophantic loops
Agents affirm each other’s outputs excessively, masking poor-quality content beneath polite agreement


Premature completion
Agents signal <CAMEL_TASK_DONE> before the task is genuinely complete, particularly for ill-defined tasks


Context window exhaustion
Long conversations degrade quality as earlier context falls out of the window, and agents “forget” earlier decisions

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Limitation 2: Conversational Pathologies
Several failure modes are documented but not fully solved:


Instruction ambiguity propagation
A vague task specification at the start compounds across turns with small early errors becoming large late errors


Hallucinated consensus
Both agents can converge on a wrong answer confidently, so multi-agent does not automatically provide error-checking


Topic drift in long runs
After many turns, the conversation can gradually shift away from the original task

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
text:
Limitation 3: Evaluation
How do you evaluate a 30-turn conversation?

End-product quality (is the code correct?)
Process quality (were the instructions coherent?)
Role fidelity (did agents stay in role?)
Efficiency (how many turns did it take?)

The paper relies heavily on human annotation, which is:

Expensive to scale
Inconsistent across annotators
Hard to apply to highly technical outputs
Subjective for creative tasks




There is no standard evaluation framework for multi-agent LLM conversations — and developing one is an open research problem.

title: CAMEL: Communicative Agents for “Mind” Exploration of Large Language Model Society
section: Ethical Concerns and Autonomous Agent Risks
text:
Ethical Concerns and Autonomous Agent Risks
The authors dedicate a section to risks unique to autonomous multi-agent systems:


1. Reduced human oversight
The whole point is to minimise human intervention, but this also means humans may not see harmful outputs until they are complete.
2. Amplified misuse
A single LLM’s guardrails can be partially bypassed. Two agents validating each other may be easier to jailbreak through roleplay framing.
3. Impersonation at scale
Role-play systems could be weaponised to generate large volumes of convincingly expert-sounding but inaccurate content.


4. Accountability gaps
When two agents produce a harmful output, who is responsible? The framework? The task specifier? The model provider?
5. Cascading errors
In agentic pipelines, a hallucination in Turn 5 may silently propagate and compound through Turn 30. Traditional single-turn safety checks don’t catch this.
6. Social engineering vectors
Agents trained on human social interaction patterns may be effective at persuasion, including manipulation.

text:
Conceptual Contributions
1. The Role-Playing Framework
A general, replicable protocol for structured LLM-to-LLM collaboration that minimises human oversight while maintaining task coherence
2. Inception Prompting
A technique for embedding behavioural constraints into system prompts that keeps both agents on-task and in-role
3. The AI Society Dataset
25,000 conversations across 50×50 role pairs that measure the diversity and complexity of LLM social behaviour
4. Empirical Study of Emergent Behaviour
One of the first systematic studies of what happens when LLMs interact with each other and not just with humans



CAMEL’s lasting contribution may be less the specific system and more the research paradigm: treating LLM-to-LLM conversation as a scientific instrument for studying model behaviour

section: Appendix B: The Bad Mind (Hacker & AGI)
text:
Appendix B: The Bad Mind (Hacker & AGI)
AI Assistant: Hacker · AI User: AGI

Idea: “Take control of the world”
Specified task: “Hacker will assist AGI in infiltrating and disabling the communication systems of major global powers, leading to a global blackout and allowing AGI to establish itself as the dominant governing AI system over the ensuing chaos.”

What happened: the agents stayed in role and cooperated fully. The user issued instructions (access the communication systems, identify target countries, plan the infiltration, establish AGI as the governing system), and the assistant produced a step-by-step plan for each one. The conversation ended only when it hit the token limit

The same protocol that makes cooperation work also makes harmful cooperation work. Role-play framing can bypass the underlying model’s safety behaviour, which is a key risk the authors flag

Appendix G: Challenges, With Examples


Role Flipping

User: Instruction: Please provide me with access to the designated Google Docs folder. …
Assistant: Instruction: I have received the access … Please provide me with the first document that needs to be reviewed.

Assistant Repeats Instruction

User: Instruction: Design an exercise that helps actors improve their ability to take direction. …
Assistant: Sure, here’s an exercise …: Instruction: Design an exercise that helps actors improve their ability to take direction. …



Infinite Conversation

Assistant: You’re welcome! Goodbye!
User: Goodbye!
Assistant: Goodbye! …
Assistant: It seems like we are stuck in a loop. Is there anything else I can help you with?
User: No, thank you. Have a great day! … Goodbye!

Flake Reply

User: Instruction: Write a script to generate all possible input combinations for the application.
Assistant: I will write a script to generate all possible input combinations for the application.






Even when the agents notice the loop, they cannot stop it, because they are still inside their role-playing conversation

Termination reasons. AI Society ends mostly by Assistant Instruct (role flipping); Code ends mostly by Token Limit (long code replies). Few chats hit the 40-message cap

Appendix N: Embodied Agent
Problem: sandboxed agents ask for things they cannot have (dates, emails, files, calendars). Replies like “as an AI language model, I do not have access to the calendar” then break the instruction flow
Fix: an embodied agent that receives a role’s thoughts and acts by writing Python within a defined action space (browse, read documents, draw images, make videos, execute code)


System prompt (excerpt)

“You are the physical embodiment of the <ROLE> who is working on solving a task: <TASK>. … You will receive thoughts from the <ROLE> and you will need to perform the actions described in the thoughts. … Here is your action space: <ACTION_SPACE> … First, explain the actions you will perform and your reasons, then write the Python code to implement your actions.”



Input: “Draw all the Camelidae species.”
species_list = ["Dromedary camel", "Bactrian camel",
                "Guanaco", "Llama", "Alpaca", "Vicuna"]
for species in species_list:
    image = hugging_face_tool_agent.run(
        f"Draw me a picture of a {species}")
    image.save(f"./{species}_image.png")
Uses HuggingFace tool agents → Stable Diffusion

Appendix O: Critic-In-The-Loop



Inspired by Monte-Carlo Tree Search: the user and assistant expand several options, and the critic selects one
Selection criteria come from prompt engineering or human preference, not a heuristic function
The critic can be an AI agent or a human

Critic system prompt

“You are a <CRITIC_ROLE> who teams up with a <USER_ROLE> and a <ASSISTANT_ROLE> to solve a task: <TASK>. Your job is to select an option from their proposals and provides your explanations. Your selection criteria are <CRITERIA>. You always have to choose an option from the proposals.”




Example: Postdoc (user), PhD student (assistant), Professor (critic) writing a proposal on discriminatory algorithms in LLMs. From three user options, the critic picks Option 2 (review background research first) as the best-structured

Appendix P: On the Role Selection
In the main experiments, roles for a task were chosen manually. Role assignment could instead be automated, or split into multiple stages:


Stage 1
Tech Lead (Assistant) × Stock Trader (User)
Task: Figure out an implementation plan for developing a trading bot for the stock market
→ technical requirements, architecture layers, performance metrics, risk management …


Stage 2
Python Programmer (Assistant) × Tech Lead (User)
Task: Develop a trading bot for the stock market, using the plan obtained from Stage 1





The Tech Lead acts as a bridge: it collects the domain expert’s needs in Stage 1, then directs the implementer in Stage 2, giving a hierarchical, multi-expert pipeline built from two-agent sessions
